<document>
# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
Sections 1–5 are strong. Each correction is documented, and most of the arithmetic checks out. The comment goes wrong when it moves from "the gain is much smaller than reported" to "the gain is entirely an artifact." The evidence it presents doesn't support that step, and some of it, including the Varden trial it relies on elsewhere, points the other way.

## 1. What holds up

**The attrition finding is the most important new fact here.** The working paper said the nine withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons." The microdata reportedly show:
- seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had started;
- six cited workload or inability to maintain output.

If that is accurate, the working paper misdescribed its own attrition, which is a serious problem.

**The output and hours corrections are well documented.**
- In 19 of 23 organisations, the manager-reported index exceeded the index computed from records.
- In the 27 organisations with time-tracking, actual hours fell 14.1%, not 20%.

**Arithmetic I've verified:**
- 34.6/40.3 is a fall of 14.1%, and 34.8/40.4 is a fall of 13.9%.
- The Table 2 rows: 98.7/0.8 = +23.4%, 95.1/0.8 = +18.9%, 98.4/0.859 = +14.6%, and 95.4/0.861 = +10.8%.
- Real revenue: 1.014/1.041 is a fall of 2.6%.
- The conclusion's "roughly four points" (output) and "roughly six points" (hours, 20 − 14.1) are both right.

**The sectoral critique is correct.** Any output index above 80 shows as a per-hour gain when hours are cut 20%, so "gains in every sector" proves nothing.

## 2. Numerical and internal problems

**The hours breakdown doesn't add up.** Pilot scheduled hours were 32. The components the comment reports are +0.7 h/day on four days (2.8 h) and 1.6 h on the day off, which gives about 36.4 h. Even measured against baseline day length (40.3/5 = 8.06 h), it comes to about 36.6 h. The reported pilot average is 34.6 h. Either the +0.7 h/day figure is wrong or it means something else. The total of 34.6 can't be checked against its parts.

**Exit reasons cover only eight of the nine withdrawals.** Six cited workload and two cited scheduling, so one is unaccounted for.

**The abstract claims a correction that was never made.** It says that "correcting the first three" problems (attrition, output, hours) reduces the gain to 10.8%. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is not corrected anywhere. The 10.8% is still an estimate among the survivors, as Section 6 concedes.

**The novelty extrapolation is off.** A straight line through +0.61 SD at month three and +0.29 SD at month six reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten." Projecting a trend from two points is also fragile.

## 3. "Entirely an artifact" is not supported

**The comment's own corrections leave a gain.** Correcting output and hours reduces the gain to about 11%, not zero. Everything after that rests on the novelty argument.

**Plausible attrition can't remove the remaining gain.** The comment shows that attrition biases the estimate upward but never estimates by how much, although the microdata would allow a bound. As a rough check, with equal weights and taking 10.8% as representative of the survivors, the nine withdrawals would need an average per-hour change of about −73% to bring the overall figure to zero. That is implausible. Employee weights could change this, so the authors should report a proper bound.

**The novelty argument uses energy as a stand-in for output, even though output data exist.**
- The decline is in self-reported *energy*, not output.
- The pilot's output index was completed **monthly**. The microdata should therefore show whether output per hour fell between months three and six. That is the direct test of novelty, and the comment doesn't run it.
- Asserting that "the burden of proof lies with those claiming [durability]" doesn't count as evidence for the opposite claim.

**The comment cites Varden selectively.**
- It calls Varden's counter-office result "the most reliable finding in the literature."
- The same trial's case-processing stratum found +12.5% output per actual hour (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4).
- That estimate meets nearly every standard the comment itself recommends: randomised, record-based output, actual hours from timesheets, and analysis of all enrolled offices.
- It was measured at nine months, beyond the point where the comment's extrapolation says energy would be back at baseline.

That estimate is the strongest evidence in the literature against "entirely an artifact," and the comment doesn't engage with it. Varden can't rule out novelty either, because staff knew their assignment and nine months is still short. But "not yet shown to be durable" is a much weaker claim than "entirely an artifact."

**Revenue partly cuts against the comment.** If real revenue fell 2.6% while actual hours fell about 14%, real revenue per actual hour rose about 13% (0.974/0.861). That isn't a productivity measure, as the comment says, and it may not cover the same organisations as the time-tracking subset. But it doesn't depend on manager ratings, and it points the same way as the residual gain.

Smaller points on revenue:
- Consumer prices are a rough deflator for organisations' revenue. The prices these organisations charge may have moved differently.
- Revenue was reported by only 52 of the 61 organisations.

**The conclusion generalises from one pilot to every scheme.** "The per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes" overall can't be judged from a re-analysis of one pilot.

## 4. Section 7 misdescribes the Varden meetings analysis

- **"Selected for analysis after the results were known."** Varden says the meeting data were collected in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results.
- **"Suggest this as a mechanism."** Varden says the analysis "cannot establish a mechanism," flags that it was not registered, and has registered a confirmatory test.
- The criticism that seven offices is a tiny sample is fair, but Varden already makes it.
- The meetings hypothesis also bears on the comment's own argument. If cutting low-value meetings drives part of the gain, that mechanism doesn't depend on novelty and could persist. The Halden interviews point the same way: 47 of 58 managers mentioned shorter or fewer meetings. The comment should treat this as an alternative it has to rule out, not set it aside.

## 5. Smaller points

- **Retail.** "Fell by 11.2%" in the three retail organisations with records rests on n = 3. The comparison with Varden's −11.4% sets a per-organisation output index against a per-FTE estimate from a randomised trial. The direction matches, but the precision of the two figures doesn't.
- **Subsets.** The Data note correctly says the subsets aren't random. Organisations with both time-tracking and submitted records may be better managed than the rest. The direction of that bias is unclear, so it adds uncertainty either way rather than supporting the comment's conclusion.

## Bottom line

**Supported:**
- The Halden 23.4% figure is substantially overstated.
- Attrition was misdescribed and was not random.
- Manager-reported output runs high.
- Scheduled hours exaggerate the reduction in time.
- Coverage-bound work loses output.
- Six months can't establish durability.

**Not supported:**
- that the remaining gain of about 11% is a novelty effect, since the monthly output data that could test this aren't used;
- that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact," which ignores Varden's case-processing result and the comment's own residual estimate.

A defensible conclusion would be roughly: "After correction, the gain is around 11% in a non-random subset of survivors. Its durability is untested, and the only randomised evidence suggests a gain of similar size in backlog-type work over nine months."

**Most useful additions:**
1. a bound on the effect of attrition;
2. the monthly trend in output per hour from the microdata;
3. an explanation of the hours breakdown;
4. a direct response to Varden's case-processing estimate.

If useful, I can draft a referee report or a reply from the Halden authors.
